svg.text: EKS Cluster Anatomy — what runs where, and its "cast"
Every app = a Pod + its supporting cast (Deployment · ServiceAccount · RBAC · ConfigMap · Service), grouped in a namespace. Helm installs the whole cast.
☁️ AWS — OUTSIDE the cluster (created by Terraform / by the LB Controller)
IAM OIDC provider
oidc.tf · the IRSA trust anchor
"AWS, trust tokens from this cluster"
IAM role + policy
lb-controller.tf
what the LB Controller may do in AWS
NLB (public subnet)
internet entry point
created by the LB Controller when NGINX asks
☸️ EKS CLUSTER — your 2 worker nodes (the control plane is AWS-managed & hidden)
📁 namespace: kube-system — cluster plumbing (auto) + the LB Controller (you, B2)
aws-node (VPC CNI)
DaemonSet · 2 pods (1/node)
gives every pod a real VPC IP
AUTO-installed
kube-proxy
DaemonSet · 2 pods (1/node)
routes ClusterIP → pod
AUTO-installed
coredns
Deployment · 2 pods
DNS: name → ClusterIP
AUTO-installed
aws-load-balancer-controller ← YOU installed (B2, via Helm)
Deployment · 2 pods (HA) · JOB: watches Services/Ingresses → creates & continuously syncs AWS NLBs/ALBs
its supporting CAST (installed by the Helm chart):
ServiceAccount
the pod's K8s identity,
ANNOTATED with the IAM
role ARN → activates IRSA
= keyless AWS creds
RBAC
ClusterRole + Binding
= what it may do INSIDE
K8s (watch svc/ingress)
≠ IAM (that's AWS)
webhook Service
a stable address for its
admission webhook (validates
Ingress objects you create)
creates & syncs ↑
📁 namespace: ingress-nginx — the NGINX router (you, B2)
ingress-nginx-controller ← YOU installed (B2, via Helm)
Deployment · 1 pod · JOB: reads your ingress.yaml → routes HTTP by path (/api→backend, /→frontend)
its supporting CAST:
ServiceAccount
its K8s identity
(no IAM needed)
RBAC
may watch Ingresses
& Services
ConfigMap
NGINX settings
(tuning/config)
Service — type: LoadBalancer ⭐
THIS is what triggers the NLB above.
The LB Controller sees it → builds the NLB.
📁 namespace: wanderlust — YOUR APP
⏳ NOT yet — ArgoCD deploys this later from your Git repo
frontend
Deployment + pod
+ frontend-service
(ClusterIP :5173)
serves the React SPA
backend
Deployment + pod
+ backend-service
(ClusterIP :8080)
the Node API
mongo
Deployment + pod
+ mongo-service (ClusterIP)
+ PVC → PV (EBS)
the database + storage
redis
Deployment + pod
+ redis-service (ClusterIP)
the cache
📁 namespace: argocd — the GitOps delivery engine
⏳ NOT yet — you install it, then IT deploys the wanderlust app above
7 pods: argocd-server (UI/API) · repo-server (renders manifests) · application-controller (the brain) · redis · dex · notifications · applicationset
JOB: watches your Git repo → applies the kubernetes/ manifests into the wanderlust namespace → keeps cluster = Git
(each of these pods ALSO has its own cast — SA, RBAC, ConfigMaps — bundled by the ArgoCD install)
📁 default · kube-node-lease · kube-public
internal bookkeeping / empty — you don't deploy here (your app goes in its own "wanderlust" namespace)
🔵 How a request flows through all this (once everything is up)
① internet → NLB (public subnet) → ② ingress-nginx-controller Service (type LoadBalancer) → ③ NGINX pod reads ingress.yaml
④ /api → backend-service → backend pod | / → frontend-service → frontend pod
⑤ backend pod → mongo-service → mongo pod (and redis-service → redis pod), all internal ClusterIP
The AWS LB Controller isn't in this live path — it just BUILT the NLB and keeps its target list pointed at the live NGINX pods.
CoreDNS resolves the service NAMES → ClusterIPs; kube-proxy does each ClusterIP → pod hop; VPC CNI gave every pod its IP.
Plumbing (CNI/kube-proxy/CoreDNS) is invisible glue that makes all the arrows above actually work.
🎭 The "cast" — every app brings these
Deployment — the supervisor that keeps N pods
running, restarts them, rolls out updates.
Pod — the actual running container (the app).
ServiceAccount — the pod's ID badge inside
Kubernetes. For IRSA it's linked to an IAM role,
so the pod also gets an AWS identity.
RBAC (ClusterRole + Binding) — what that badge
may DO inside K8s (e.g. "watch Services").
This is K8s permissions — NOT the same as IAM.
ConfigMap — the app's settings file, injected
into the pod (config without rebuilding the image).
Service — a stable network address for the pod(s):
• ClusterIP = internal only
• LoadBalancer = asks AWS for an external LB ⭐
Why it repeats: each app is independent, so each
brings its own cast. Helm bundles it into one chart,
so "install chart" = pod + SA + RBAC + ConfigMap +
Service, all at once.
IAM ≠ RBAC: IAM = AWS permissions (create an NLB);
RBAC = Kubernetes permissions (read an Ingress).
⏱️ What's in the cluster — NOW vs LATER
After terraform apply (B1 + B2):
✅ kube-system: CNI, kube-proxy, CoreDNS
✅ kube-system: AWS LB Controller (2 pods)
✅ ingress-nginx: NGINX controller (1 pod)
✅ AWS: the NLB + IAM OIDC/role
After you install ArgoCD:
➕ argocd namespace (7 pods)
After ArgoCD syncs your Git repo:
➕ wanderlust namespace (frontend, backend,
mongo, redis) + the Ingress goes live
So right now the app is NOT there yet — the
controllers + plumbing come first.
🧱 The layers (memorize this shape)
Layer 4 YOUR APP — frontend/backend/mongo/redis
Layer 3 DELIVERY — ArgoCD (GitOps)
Layer 2 TRAFFIC-IN — NGINX + AWS LB Controller
Layer 1 PLUMBING — CNI · kube-proxy · CoreDNS
Layer 0 NODES — 2× EC2 worker nodes
Layer-1 AWS EDGE — NLB + IAM (OIDC/role)
Control plane (apiserver/scheduler/etcd) is
AWS-managed & hidden — never in this picture.
Wanderlust on EKS · cluster anatomy & the supporting cast · pairs with the two request-flow diagrams
Node-by-Node View — Control Plane vs each Worker Node
In EKS, `kubectl get nodes` shows ONLY the 2 worker nodes — the control plane is AWS-managed and hidden. Node-level processes (kubelet, containerd) are NOT pods.
🧠 CONTROL PLANE — AWS-managed & HIDDEN · not in `kubectl get nodes` · runs across 3 AZs (HA) · flat $0.10/hr
kube-apiserver — the front door
kubectl AND every component talk ONLY to this. Nothing talks
to anything else directly — the apiserver is the single hub.
For each request it runs: authentication → authorization
(RBAC) → admission control → then reads/writes etcd.
🎯 It is the ONLY component that talks to etcd. Stateless, so
it scales horizontally. "Everything goes through the apiserver."
how it connects: receives your YAML, stores desired state,
and serves it to scheduler/kubelet/controllers that watch it.
etcd — the cluster database
A distributed key-value store holding EVERY object in the
cluster (pods, services, secrets, configmaps…). The single
source of truth — "desired state" lives here.
🎯 The ONLY stateful component. Needs odd-number quorum
(3 or 5) for HA. Back it up — lose etcd = lose the cluster.
EKS runs & backs it up for you.
how it connects: only the apiserver reads/writes it; no other
component touches etcd directly.
kube-scheduler — places pods
Watches the apiserver for new pods with no node yet. Picks
the best node using: resource requests, taints/tolerations,
node/pod affinity, topology spread.
🎯 It only WRITES the node assignment — it does NOT start
the pod. "Scheduler places, kubelet runs." Uses requests,
not limits, to decide fit.
how it connects: reads unscheduled pods from apiserver,
writes the chosen node back to apiserver.
kube-controller-manager — the reconcile loops
A bundle of ~30 controllers, each running a loop that makes ACTUAL state match DESIRED state. Examples:
• Deployment controller → creates ReplicaSets → which create Pods (keeps N replicas alive)
• Node controller → marks a node NotReady / evicts pods if a node dies
• Endpoints controller → keeps each Service's list of healthy pod IPs up to date
🎯 This is the "controller/operator pattern" at the core of Kubernetes: watch desired, observe actual, act to close the gap.
If you delete a pod of a Deployment, THIS is what notices and recreates it.
how it connects: watches + writes objects through the apiserver (never etcd directly).
Interview framing: "the controller-manager is why Kubernetes is declarative and self-healing."
cloud-controller-manager — the AWS bridge
Holds all the cloud-provider-specific logic, kept OUT of core Kubernetes. On EKS it integrates with AWS to:
• provision an ELB/NLB when you create a Service of type=LoadBalancer (the in-tree path)
• manage node lifecycle (delete the Node object when its EC2 instance is terminated)
• set up routes / attach volumes via the cloud APIs
🎯 This is the historical way Service type=LoadBalancer got an AWS LB. The modern, richer way is the
AWS Load Balancer Controller (a pod YOU install) — which is why we installed it for NLBs/ALBs.
how it connects: watches Services/Nodes via apiserver, calls AWS APIs to make reality match.
On EKS all of the above control-plane pieces are AWS-managed — you never SSH in or scale them.
You never patch or scale any of these — AWS does. In self-managed Kubernetes (kubeadm) you'd run all 5 yourself on a dedicated control-plane node.
🔵 Interview classic: "what happens when you kubectl apply a Deployment?" — follow the arrows across control plane → node
kubectl → ① apiserver (authN → authZ/RBAC → admission) → ② stores desired state in etcd → ③ controller-manager creates ReplicaSet → Pod objects →
④ scheduler assigns each Pod a node → ⑤ that node's kubelet sees "a pod is mine" → ⑥ kubelet tells containerd to pull the image & run it →
⑦ kubelet reports status back to the apiserver → etcd. The control plane plans; the node runs. Live user traffic never touches this path.
🖥️ Worker Node 1 — ip-172-31-33-239
a REAL EC2 VM · c7i-flex.large · 2 vCPU / ~3.07 GiB allocatable · us-east-2c · shows up in `kubectl get nodes`
① Node PROCESSES — run directly on the OS, NOT pods
kubelet — the node's agent (a systemd process)
Watches the apiserver for pods assigned to THIS node, then tells containerd to run them. Reports pod + node
health back to the apiserver, and runs liveness/readiness probes. cAdvisor (inside kubelet) gives container metrics.
🎯 It watches the API SERVER, not etcd. It is a PROCESS on the node, not a pod. "Scheduler places, kubelet runs."
how it connects: apiserver ⇄ kubelet ⇄ containerd. If kubelet dies, the node goes NotReady.
containerd — the container runtime (a process)
Pulls images and actually runs the containers. kubelet talks to it through the CRI (Container Runtime Interface).
🎯 Docker was replaced by containerd — "dockershim" was removed in Kubernetes 1.24. Path: kubelet → CRI → containerd → runc → container.
② DaemonSet PODS — exactly 1 per node (so EVERY node has these)
aws-node (Amazon VPC CNI)
Gives every pod ON THIS NODE a real, routable VPC IP (from ENIs attached to the EC2 instance).
🎯 This is why an ALB can target pod IPs directly, and why pods-per-node is capped by ENIs/IPs (29 here).
"Prefix delegation" raises that pod cap. The CNI is what makes pod networking work at all.
kube-proxy
Programs THIS node's iptables / IPVS rules so a Service's ClusterIP:port is rewritten to a real pod IP.
🎯 kube-proxy is HOW a virtual ClusterIP actually reaches a pod. It runs on every node and does the node→pod hop.
It reads the Endpoints (healthy pod IPs) the control plane maintains, and keeps its local rules in sync.
③ Scheduled PODS — the scheduler happened to place these here
coredns × 2 (both landed on Node 1 in your real cluster)
Cluster DNS: resolves Service NAMES → ClusterIP (e.g. backend-service → 10.100.x.x).
🎯 It's a Deployment (2 pods), NOT per-node — the scheduler can put both on one node, as it did here.
aws-load-balancer-controller (1 of its 2 HA replicas)
Talks OUT to AWS to create/sync NLBs & ALBs. Uses IRSA (its ServiceAccount → IAM role) for AWS creds.
Its 2 replicas usually spread across both nodes for high availability.
your app pods — LATER (ArgoCD)
frontend / backend / mongo / redis will be scheduled across both nodes once ArgoCD deploys them.
The scheduler decides which node each lands on — and it doesn't matter, networking abstracts location.
🖥️ Worker Node 2 — ip-172-31-7-0
a REAL EC2 VM · c7i-flex.large · 2 vCPU / ~3.07 GiB allocatable · also in `kubectl get nodes`
① Node PROCESSES — identical role to Node 1 (every node has these)
kubelet — the node agent (process)
Same job as on Node 1: watches the apiserver for pods assigned to THIS node and runs them via containerd,
reports health, runs probes. Each node has its OWN kubelet — it only manages its own node's pods.
🎯 Every worker node runs its own kubelet + containerd. They're the two things that make a machine a "node".
how it connects: apiserver ⇄ this node's kubelet ⇄ this node's containerd.
containerd — the container runtime (process)
Same as Node 1: pulls images, runs containers via the CRI. Independent per node.
🎯 A "node" = a VM running kubelet + a container runtime + kube-proxy + CNI. That combo is the minimum to join a cluster.
② DaemonSet PODS — again, exactly 1 per node
aws-node (VPC CNI)
This node's own copy — assigns VPC IPs to pods running on Node 2. (A DaemonSet guarantees one per node.)
🎯 DaemonSet = "run exactly one copy of this pod on every node" (used for per-node agents: CNI, kube-proxy, log/metric agents).
Add a 3rd node → the DaemonSet automatically puts an aws-node + kube-proxy on it too.
kube-proxy
This node's own copy — programs Node 2's iptables/IPVS so ClusterIP traffic landing here reaches a pod.
🎯 Any node can receive traffic for any Service and relay it to a pod anywhere — because every node runs kube-proxy.
This is why "hit any node, it routes correctly" works (the NodePort lesson).
③ Scheduled PODS — placed here by the scheduler
aws-load-balancer-controller (the other HA replica)
The 2nd of the 2 replicas — spread here for high availability (if Node 1 dies, this one keeps managing LBs).
🎯 2 replicas on different nodes = survives a single node failure. Standard HA pattern for controllers.
ingress-nginx-controller (1 pod)
Receives traffic from the NLB and routes by path (/api → backend, / → frontend) per your ingress.yaml.
Scale it to 2+ replicas in production for HA; here 1 is fine for learning.
your app pods — LATER (ArgoCD)
Some of frontend/backend/mongo/redis will land here too — the scheduler balances across both nodes.
e.g. backend pod on Node 1 AND Node 2 → the Service load-balances across both.
🏭 What REAL production clusters also run on every node (industry-grade — not in this basic cluster yet)
• node-exporter (DaemonSet) — node CPU/RAM/disk metrics for Prometheus. • kube-state-metrics — object/state metrics.
• fluent-bit / fluentd (DaemonSet) — ships container logs to CloudWatch/ELK/Loki. • Datadog / OTEL agent (DaemonSet) — APM + metrics + traces.
• EBS / EFS CSI driver — lets PVCs provision real AWS volumes (MongoDB needs this). • Falco (DaemonSet) — runtime security.
• Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter — watch for unschedulable pods and ADD nodes automatically (then remove idle ones).
🎯 Pattern to remember: anything that must run "once on every node" (agents for logs, metrics, security, networking) ships as a DaemonSet.
Node scaling itself is done by Cluster Autoscaler (older) or Karpenter (newer, AWS-native) — a top Dublin interview topic.
